analysis.one_liner: Requires meat packers to publicly report their own cattle holdings and improves price information for ranchers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with three Senate Democrats behind it, was sent to the Agriculture Committee in July 1996 and died there without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced large meatpacking companies to disclose, within 24 hours, the cattle they own or control through contracts — so-called "captive supply" — and to report prices in local and regional markets. It would have directed the Agriculture Department to monitor packers for anticompetitive behavior, required good-faith bargaining with farmer cooperatives, and required clearer labeling of imported meat. It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and never came up again.
analysis.who_benefits: Cattle ranchers and family livestock producers, who would see the volume of packer-owned or contract cattle and prices in their own markets, giving them real information when they sell. Consumers would get clearer labeling showing whether meat was imported. Farmer cooperatives would gain a legal right to good-faith negotiations with buyers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cattle ranchers and family livestock producers

how_it_helps.text: Defines "captive supply" — cattle a packer owns, feeds, finances, or holds under forward contracts — and requires the Agriculture Department to make information on those transactions public within 24 hours, so ranchers can see how much of the market packers already control before they sell.

Requires public annual reporting of livestock marketed and slaughtered nationally and in regional and local markets, with a significant share of local transactions covered, giving sellers price data at the point of sale.

Directs the Agriculture Department to monitor anticompetitive behavior among packers, stockyard owners, and dealers and report findings to Congress, the Attorney General, and the public, and to coordinate antitrust enforcement with the Justice Department.
Makes it an unfair trade practice for buyers to refuse good-faith negotiations with producer cooperatives, strengthening family farmers' collective bargaining position.
Requires imported meat that is graded to carry labels stating it was imported or contains imported meat, so shoppers know the origin of what they buy.
Creates a commission to study packer concentration's effect on cattle prices, meat grading, and value-added products, reporting to Congress by January 2000.

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking companies, which would bear the cost of reporting every captive-supply transaction within 24 hours and face public antitrust monitoring for the first time in this form, and meat importers, which would have to label graded imported products.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large meatpacking companies and meat importers

drawbacks.text: The bill carries real compliance costs: packers would have to report nearly every captive-supply transaction within 24 hours, and part of that cost would likely be passed back to producers through lower bids.

Much of the bill turns on the Agriculture Department's own discretion — the definition of captive supply is "as determined by the Secretary," and the monitoring provisions rely on the Department requesting its own additional funding — so its strength would depend entirely on how vigorously the administration of the day enforced it.

The proposed livestock industry commission would be made up of nongovernmental members chosen in consultation with industry representatives, which raises the risk that it studies packer concentration without changing anything.

Publishing transaction details within 24 hours while preserving the confidentiality of individual transactions is a difficult balance, and an early version of such data systems could have exposed some producers' contract terms to competitors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: transparency about who controls cattle supply and what prices are being paid, in exchange for paperwork costs borne mainly by the largest packers. The information and labeling provisions would give ranchers and consumers facts they did not have, and the costs fall on a highly concentrated industry — four large firms dominated beef packing at the time. The bill's weaknesses are that it relies on discretionary agency enforcement and creates a study commission rather than binding new limits on packer ownership, so even if enacted its teeth would have depended on follow-through.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or a vote before Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Senator Kent Conrad of North Dakota introduced the bill on July 10, 1996, joined by Senators Byron Dorgan and Robert Kerrey, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day.
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action — before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, at which point the bill died.
The bill's cosponsors were three Democrats, and no Republican signed on, so it never had the support base to force its way onto the committee agenda.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large meatpacking companies came out ahead: captive-supply deals stayed out of public view, prices in local markets went unreported, and no new antitrust monitoring or import labeling was imposed.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, but no vote was ever taken, so the partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would have forced packers to disclose their captive cattle holdings within 24 hours and face public USDA antitrust monitoring, ending the information advantage that comes from knowing how much supply they already control while ranchers do not. Beef packing was highly concentrated, so a handful of firms bore the whole cost.

Producers would have gained price information at the point of sale, public captive-supply data, good-faith bargaining rights for cooperatives, and a federal eye on anticompetitive conduct — tools for getting a fairer price when they sell.
Imported graded meat would have had to carry labels stating it was imported or contained imported meat, removing the option of selling foreign product without telling shoppers where it came from.
The Agricultural Fair Practices Act would have been amended to make refusing good-faith negotiations with farmer cooperatives an unfair trade practice, giving cooperatives legal leverage with buyers.
